Milkfish, Chanos chanos, begin their lives as small, transparent eggs that drift in the warm pelagic waters of the tropical Indo-Pacific. At a constant temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the embryonic development proceeds rapidly, leading to eclosion approximately 1.5 days  after fertilization. The newly emerged prolarvae, still heavily dependent on their internal yolk reserves, measure a mere 0.35 cm  in total length at hatch. This minuscule size is typical of teleost larvae that embark on a planktonic existence immediately upon emergence. Within a few days of absorbing their yolk sac and commencing first exogenous feeding, these larvae have grown only slightly, reaching about 0.5 cm [Lb = about 0.5 cm] in total length at birth, a term often used by aquaculturists to denote the point of first feeding. The post-hatching development is critically dependent on water temperature; under stable 29 °C conditions, the yolk is rapidly metabolized, powering organogenesis and the opening of the mouth. The onset of exogenous feeding occurs approximately 6.5 days [ab = approximately 6.5 days] after fertilization at this temperature at a temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C].

During their first weeks of life, the larvae undergo rapid morphological differentiation while inhabiting coastal and estuarine nurseries. Under the same warm regime (29 °C [T = 29 °C]), the larval body plan begins to reorganize approximately 20.5 days  after fertilization, marking the onset of larval metamorphosis. This transformation, which involves the ossification of fin rays and the development of a more streamlined, fusiform body shape, signifies the transition from a planktonic larva to a bottom-oriented juvenile. In the wild, this period is often associated with a habitat shift from open water to shallow, productive mangrove swamps and tidal flats where food is abundant. The timing of metamorphosis is tightly linked to warm, stable temperatures that accelerate growth and enzymatic processes. The success of this larval-juvenile transition is a key bottleneck in the species' life history, determining subsequent recruitment into the adult population.

As milkfish mature, they exhibit a remarkable capacity for growth, eventually reaching extraordinarily large body sizes. The ultimate total length, a measure of the maximum size a fish can attain under favorable conditions, can reach up to 170 cm [Li = up to 170 cm] from the snout to the tip of the tail. Corresponding to this impressive linear dimension, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is reported to be around 14,000 grams [Wwi = around 14,000 grams], representing the peak of somatic investment. Such substantial size is characteristic of a large, fast-growing fish that occupies a high trophic position in its ecosystem, where it feeds primarily on algae and detritus. This maximum weight is not attained until after many years of sustained growth during the juvenile and sub-adult phases. Reaching this asymptotic body size requires a long-term commitment of resources to structural growth and tissue repair, a pattern common among large-bodied tropical marine fishes that experience high survival rates in the absence of intense fishing pressure. In the family Chanidae, such large body dimensions place it among the larger herbivorous teleosts.

Sexual maturity in milkfish is attained after a prolonged juvenile period, with individuals typically reaching the pubertal stage when they have achieved a specific body size. The total length at puberty, which marks the onset of gonadal development and the ability to reproduce, has been determined to be approximately 65 cm [Lp = approximately 65 cm]. At this length, the fish have also accumulated considerable somatic mass, requiring a wet weight at puberty of about 4,500 grams [Wwp = about 4,500 grams] to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis. The journey to this reproductive threshold is a slow one, taking approximately three years after hatching [tR = approximately three years after hatching] for the first successful spawning event to occur, and this occurs reliably under the warm thermal regime of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. This relatively extended pre-reproductive phase is a common life-history strategy among large fishes, allowing for ample time to accumulate the necessary energy reserves before diverting resources toward reproduction.

The longevity and reproductive output of milkfish are impressive, reflecting an adaptation to a stable tropical environment with low natural mortality. The maximum documented life span for the species is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. Towards the end of this period, natural senescence sets in, leading to a decline in physiological function. Throughout their adult lives, mature females display a high fecundity. A single large gravid female weighing about 6,000 grams can release an estimated 3.5 million eggs per year [Ri = 3.5 million eggs per year], consistent with an annual spawning cycle during the warmest months. This massive reproductive output is a hallmark of a highly fecund species, ensuring robust recruitment into the larval pool even in variable coastal environments.
